notToBeConfusedWith.name: Aperol
notToBeConfusedWith.note: From the same owner and the same shelf, and not interchangeable: roughly half the strength, considerably sweeter and far less bitter.

notToBeConfusedWith.name: Bitter
notToBeConfusedWith.note: The generic category name in Italy, where several producers make one; a recipe naming Campari means this bottle rather than the category.

generalSubstitutes.note: Lower in strength and higher in sugar, so a drink built on it comes out longer, sweeter and much less bitter. Widely done, and closer to a different drink than to a substitution.

forms.label: Standard
forms.animalOriginNote: The red was carmine, a colourant made from insects, until the producer moved to synthetic colourants in the mid-2000s. The European label cached here lists E122, E102 and E133 and no carmine, and the United States bottling uses Red 40; reporting on the change describes it as not having reached every market at once, so which colourant is in a given bottle depends on where it was made.
forms.sourceNote: The producer's own consumer-information page states 25% alc./vol. and, per 1.5 fl oz serving, 108 calories and 11.5 g of carbohydrate; those are restated here per 100 ml. The carbohydrate is taken as sugar because the product carries no other kind. FoodData Central has no record for Campari at all. Cross-checked against the site's own energy arithmetic: 25% alcohol plus 25.9 g of sugar comes to 242 kcal against the 243 the producer publishes, which is what makes the 25% credible - an Open Food Facts entry files the same product at 20%, and at 20% the arithmetic misses by fourteen per cent.
